records.name: Helmar
records.facts_used: A signed name guide describes Helmar as a German variant of Helmer and Hilmar. Another international account continues Heilmar, with heil, whole or healthy, and mari, famous. These documented family routes remain distinct rather than becoming one compulsory explanation for every bearer. The related form’s history is illustrated by Norwegian explorer Helmer Hanssen: the Fram Museum names him among the five men who reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911. This concerns related Helmer and a Norwegian expedition rather than Helmar’s first use in Estonia.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated calendar, dictionary, linguistic, press or institutional episode support two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Signed SNL Helmar article explicitly calls it a German variant of Helmer/Hilmar; curated Helmar continues Heilmar, heil/mari. Preserve the documented family alternatives without choosing one universal route. Opened primary Fram Museum Helmer Julius Hanssen biography gives the five-man South Pole party, 14 December 1911. It is explicitly a related Helmer example from a Norwegian expedition, not a Helmar first record in Estonia. No unverified search-result bearer biography was accepted.

records.name: Helmer
records.facts_used: Helmer has several documented European explanations. German Helm-mar combines helmet and famous, while Helm-her combines helmet and warrior; a connection with Hjalmar is also recorded. A shared spelling therefore does not require one borrowing route for every family. Helmer Jõgi’s parliamentary biography supplies a concrete Estonian example. The official Riigikogu record lists service in its tenth and eleventh compositions from 2003 to 2011. This is a verifiable professional use of the exact given name rather than the date of its first appearance.

records.uncertainties: Signed SNL Helmer article gives Helm-mar helmet/famous or Helm-her helmet/warrior; curated Helmer additionally refers to Helmar/Hjalmar. Opened primary Riigikogu Helmer Jõgi biography directly gives tenth/eleventh compositions 2003–2011. Direct HTML fetch succeeded despite the web reader’s cache miss. records.name: Helmo
records.facts_used: Helmo has a documented connection with Helmut: a study of historical Estonian names places Helmo among Low German intermediary forms. The Helmut family is usually explained through helm, helmet, and muot, mind, spirit or courage. The study’s column distinctions matter for tracing this route. The table row in Evar Saar’s 2016 article reads Helmok, Helmus — Helmo, Helmke — Helmut. Its historical material comes from South Tartumaa revisions of 1582–1588. It documents a particular related-form route rather than asserting that modern Helmo was already registered there as an exact Estonian spelling.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated calendar, dictionary, linguistic, press or institutional episode support two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Visually checked EE-SAAR16 PDF p. 42 / printed p. 43 explicitly places exact Helmo as a Low German intermediary linking recorded Helmok/Helmus to Helmut. It establishes an explicit historical family correspondence, not an exact modern Estonian Helmo registration in 1582–1588. Narratives repeatedly preserve those columns. The connection is not extended to Helmu/Helmur. General user-submitted modern variants are not the evidence.

records.name: Helmut
records.facts_used: Helmut is a German two-part name, usually explained through helm, helmet, and muot, mind, spirit or courage; another account relates the first element to heil, whole or healthy. These nuances concern historical name elements rather than one compulsory sentence about a person. Evar Saar’s 2016 table of South Tartumaa names from 1582–1588 connects Helmok and Helmus with Low German Helmo and Helmke, then Helmut. This is an analysis of historical correspondences. The middle column’s German forms should retain their scope rather than becoming exact Estonian record spellings.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated calendar, dictionary, linguistic, press or institutional episode support two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Signed SNL article gives Helm-/mut helmet/courage; curated Helmut gives helm (or possibly heil) + muot mind/spirit. Preserve the documented nuance without forcing one literal sentence. Visually checked EE-SAAR16, Evar Saar (2016), PDF p. 42 / printed p. 43, Appendix 2 continuation: Helmok, Helmus | Helmo, Helmke | Helmut. The preceding appendix heading PDF p. 41 / printed p. 42 dates South Tartumaa material to 1582–1588, collected from Roslavlev’s 1970 Polnische Akten I. The middle column is Low German source forms, not exact Estonian attestation spellings; publication is 2016 despite filename VItoim16sisu.

records.name: Feliksas
records.facts_used: Feliksas is connected with Latin felix, happy or fortunate. In Roman usage Felix served as a personal cognomen and later became a widespread Christian name. The Lithuanian form preserves this name family’s Latin basis. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar lists Feliksas with short form Felis on 14 January; Salys reprinted the list in 1983. This historical calendar placement differs from the 20 November used here. It documents the pair of forms rather than the name’s creation date.
records.reason: Exact-form or explicit family evidence and a concrete dated calendar, dictionary, linguistic, press or institutional episode support two paragraphs in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Exact LT-GUIDE gives Latin felix, corroborated by curated Felix and its Roman cognomen context. Visually checked Salys PDF p. 301 / printed p. 286 gives Feliksas (Felis) on 14 JANUARY; the preceding PDF p. 300 has Sausis heading. It is the 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar reprinted in 1983, not first use. The project’s 20 November stays unchanged; Sirena 2015 front page independently supports that day.

records.name: Jovydas
records.facts_used: Jovydas is a Lithuanian two-stem name. The guide connects jo- with joti, to ride, and jotis, rider, and vyd- with (iš)vydo, saw. The elements help explain its formation without requiring one compulsory literal sentence about a rider. The 1964 Tikiu Dievą calendar gives Jovydas with short form Jovas on 20 November. The checked list was reprinted in volume two of Salys’s writings in 1983. It directly records the full/short relationship rather than proving that the name was created when the calendar appeared.

records.name: Vigo
records.facts_used: Vigo is a documented Latvian rendering of Danish Viggo. Viggo is connected with Old Norse víg, war or battle, as a short form of names containing that element. The guide’s year documents a rendering rule rather than first use of the name.
